what_its_for: Avelumab is a cancer medicine used to treat two types of cancer: Merkel cell carcinoma (a rare type of skin cancer) and a type of bladder or urinary tract cancer called urothelial carcinoma. It works by helping your immune system find and attack cancer cells.
how_to_take: Avelumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or catheter. A nurse or healthcare provider will give you this medicine at a clinic or hospital. Each infusion takes about 1 hour. Before each infusion, you will be given antihistamine and acetaminophen (Tylenol) medicines to help prevent infusion reactions. You should not try to give this medicine to yourself at home.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 800 mg given once every 2 weeks. Your doctor may adjust your dose or delay your treatment depending on how your body responds or if you have side effects. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose schedule.
missed_dose: Because avelumab is given by a healthcare provider in a clinic, your appointments are carefully scheduled. If you miss or need to reschedule an infusion appointment, call your doctor or treatment center as soon as possible to set up a new appointment. Do not try to make up for a missed dose on your own.
storage: Avelumab is stored and handled by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. You do not need to store this medicine at home. If you have any questions about how the medicine is stored, ask your healthcare team.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving any live vaccines (such as the shingles vaccine Zostavax or the nasal flu vaccine) while being treated with avelumab without first talking to your doctor. Tell your doctor before starting any new medicines, vitamins, or supplements. Avoid activities that could increase your risk of infection. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, talk to your doctor before starting treatment, as avelumab can harm an unborn baby.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: trouble breathing, chest pain, fast or irregular heartbeat, or flushing during or after your infusion (signs of an infusion reaction); severe rash, itching, or blistering skin; yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain (signs of liver problems); severe or persistent diarrhea or stomach pain (signs of intestinal problems); unusual fatigue, increased thirst, frequent urination, or weight gain or loss (signs of hormone gland problems); vision changes; severe muscle weakness or pain; signs of infection such as fever, chills, or cough. These could be signs of serious immune-related side effects that need immediate medical attention.
when_it_works: Avelumab does not work overnight. It may take several weeks to months before you notice the benefits of treatment. Some patients may respond sooner than others. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular tests and imaging scans. Continue going to all your scheduled appointments even if you do not feel different right away.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Avelumab can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 month after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 1 month after the last dose. Older adults (65 years and older): No special dose adjustment is needed, but older adults should be closely monitored for side effects. Children: The safety and effectiveness of avelumab in children younger than 12 years old have not been established. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as this may affect how you respond to treatment.
